title: Sounds and the alphabet
objectives: I can pronounce the oral vowels, the nasal vowels and the most common diphthongs of Brazilian Portuguese.
I can read the digraphs lh, nh, ch, rr, qu and gu and the sounds of letters that change with their position.
I can say the name of every letter and spell my own name aloud.
I can use written accents to find the stressed syllable and to tell open vowels from closed ones.

vocabulary.note: The stressed a is open, like the a in father. The final unstressed a is weak and short, like the a in sofa. The s between two vowels sounds like z, so the word sounds like KAH-zuh.
The acute accent shows an open é, like the e in bed, said with the mouth fairly open.

example.pt: Este é o pé do Paulo.

vocabulary.note: The circumflex shows a closed ê, like the ay in say but without the glide to an ee sound. Hold the vowel steady. The stress is on the last syllable: voh-SEH.
The acute accent shows an open ó, like the aw in law. Compare with avô, which has a closed vowel.
The circumflex shows a closed ô, like the o in go but without the w glide at the end. Hold the lips round and still.
A final unstressed o sounds like the oo in moon, but short: LEE-vroo. The r after a consonant is a very quick tap of the tongue.

example.pt: Este é o livro da Ana.

vocabulary.note: The letter u is like the oo in moon (silent only in qu and gu before e or i), never like the u in cup or in cute.
The diphthong ei sounds like ay in day. The syllable te at the end of a word sounds like chee in most of Brazil: LAY-chee.

example.pt: Este é o leite do Carlos.

vocabulary.note: The diphthong ai sounds like the English word eye. The p is not followed by a puff of air as it is in English pie.
The nasal diphthong ãe sounds like the English word my said through the nose, with no n or m sound at the end.
The nasal diphthong ão sounds like the ow in now said through the nose. The tilde marks the nasal sound. Do not pronounce a final n.
The nasal diphthong õe sounds like the oy in boy said through the nose. This is the plural of limão.
A final m is not a consonant here. It nasalizes the vowel before it, so bom sounds like the English bone with the n left off, and the lips stay open.
An n before another consonant nasalizes the vowel before it: the i sounds like the ee in see with air through the nose. The n itself is barely heard.
The digraph lh sounds like lli in million. The tongue touches the roof of the mouth in one smooth move.

example.pt: Este é o filho do Carlos.

vocabulary.note: The digraph nh sounds like ny in canyon, like the ñ in Spanish.
The digraph ch sounds like sh in shoe, never like ch in church.
A word-initial r sounds like an English h in hat, with some air from the throat. In a few regions it is a stronger rolled or scraping sound.
The double rr sounds exactly like a word-initial r, like an English h. Say it as KAH-hoo.
A single r between vowels is a quick tap of the tongue, like the tt in American English butter. Compare with carro, where rr sounds like h.
Before e or i the letters qu sound like k and the u is silent. The j sounds like the s in measure.
Before e or i the letters gu sound like the g in go and the u is silent. The rr sounds like h.
In most of Brazil a d before the vowel i sounds like the j in jeep, so dia sounds like JEE-uh. Some regions say a plain d.
In most of Brazil a t before the vowel i sounds like the ch in cheese, so tia sounds like CHEE-uh.
A letter l at the end of a syllable sounds like the English w. The word sounds like bra-ZEEW and is never said with an English l.
A single s between two vowels sounds like z, as in zoo. At the start of a word it sounds like s, as in sun.
A final s sounds like the s in sit in most of Brazil. In Rio de Janeiro and some other regions it sounds like sh.
The cedilla makes c sound like s. The ç appears only before a, o and u, and never at the start of a word.

example.pt: Esta é a cabeça do Paulo.

vocabulary.note: The ç sounds like s and the acute accent on ú marks the stressed syllable: a-SOO-kar.
At the start of a word the letter x usually sounds like sh in shoe. The acute accent marks the stress on the first syllable.

example.pt: Esta é a xícara da Ana.

vocabulary.note: The letter x has several sounds. In táxi it sounds like ks, as in the English word taxi.
The letter h is always silent. The j sounds like the s in measure, and the final e sounds like ee: OH-zhee.
Before e or i the letter g sounds like the s in measure. The final te sounds like chee: ZHEN-chee. The n nasalizes the first e.
The acute accent on é marks the stressed syllable and an open vowel. The stress is on the last syllable: ca-FEH.
The circumflex on ô marks the stressed syllable, which is the first one, and a closed vowel: OH-nee-boos.
Say ah-GAH. The letter itself is silent in words but has a name.

example.en: Hoje is spelled with an H.

vocabulary.note: Say ZHOH-tah, with the j like the s in measure.

example.en: João is spelled with a J.

vocabulary.note: The letter K is rare. It appears in foreign words and names such as Kátia.

example.en: Kátia is spelled with a K.

vocabulary.note: Say EH-hee, with the first r sounding like an English h.

example.en: Rua is spelled with an R.

vocabulary.note: Say sheess, with the x sounding like sh.

example.en: Táxi is spelled with an X.

vocabulary.note: The letter Y appears in names such as Yasmin. Some people also call it i grego.

example.en: Yasmin is spelled with a Y.

vocabulary.note: The letter W appears in foreign names such as Wagner. The acute accent marks the stress on the first syllable.

example.en: Wagner is spelled with a W.

vocabulary.en: how do you spell it, how is it written
vocabulary.note: The standard question when you want a word or name spelled out. A common answer is a list of letter names.

example.en: How do you spell the name?

vocabulary.note: Say VEH-lah with a plain l. Compare with velha, which has the lh sound.
The lh sounds like lli in million. The masculine is velho.
A plain n, as in no. Compare with sonho, which has the nh sound.
The nh sounds like ny in canyon.
The acute accent marks an open, stressed a. Compare with lã, which is nasal.
The tilde makes the a nasal: say lah through your nose, without a final n.

dialogues.title: At a hotel desk
dialogues.context: Paulo checks in at a hotel in Salvador. The receptionist asks him to spell his first name and his surname.

lines.speaker: Marina
lines.pt: Boa tarde! Como você se chama?
lines.en: Good afternoon! What is your name?

lines.speaker: Paulo
lines.pt: Boa tarde. Meu nome é Paulo.
lines.en: Good afternoon. My name is Paulo.

lines.speaker: Marina
lines.en: How do you spell it?

lines.speaker: Paulo
lines.en: P, A, U, L, O.

lines.speaker: Marina
lines.en: Thank you. And the last name?

lines.speaker: Paulo
lines.en: My last name is Teixeira.

lines.speaker: Marina
lines.en: How do you spell it, please?

lines.speaker: Paulo
lines.pt: Tê, é, i, xis, é, i, erre, á.
lines.en: T, E, I, X, E, I, R, A.

lines.speaker: Marina
lines.pt: Teixeira, com xis. Muito obrigada, senhor Teixeira!
lines.en: Teixeira, with an X. Thank you very much, Mr. Teixeira!

lines.speaker: Paulo
lines.en: You're welcome.

dialogues.title: A phone call to a restaurant
dialogues.context: Renata calls a restaurant to book a table. Bruno, who answers, has trouble hearing her name.

lines.speaker: Bruno
lines.en: Good evening, Restaurante Brasil.

lines.speaker: Renata
lines.pt: Boa noite! Meu nome é Renata.
lines.en: Good evening! My name is Renata.

lines.speaker: Bruno
lines.en: Sorry, what was that?

lines.speaker: Renata
lines.pt: Renata. Erre, é, ene, á, tê, á.
lines.en: Renata. R, E, N, A, T, A.

lines.speaker: Bruno
lines.en: Thank you, Renata. And the last name?

lines.speaker: Renata
lines.pt: Meu sobrenome é Gomes. Gê, ó, eme, é, esse.
lines.en: My last name is Gomes. G, O, M, E, S.

lines.speaker: Bruno
lines.en: Gomes, with a G. Right?

lines.speaker: Renata
lines.en: Right! Thank you.

lines.speaker: Bruno
lines.en: You're welcome, Renata. See you soon!

lines.speaker: Renata
lines.en: Bye!

dialogues.title: A spelling game in class
dialogues.context: Professora Lúcia asks two students to spell words that practice the sounds qu, gu and rr.

lines.speaker: Lúcia
lines.en: Good afternoon!

lines.speaker: João
lines.en: Good afternoon, teacher!

lines.speaker: Lúcia
lines.en: How do you spell queijo, João?

lines.speaker: João
lines.pt: Quê, u, é, i, jota, ó.
lines.en: Q, U, E, I, J, O.

lines.speaker: Lúcia
lines.en: Very good! And Brasil, Camila?

lines.speaker: Camila
lines.pt: Bê, erre, á, esse, i, ele.
lines.en: B, R, A, S, I, L.

lines.speaker: Lúcia
lines.en: Perfect! And guitarra?

lines.speaker: João
lines.pt: Gê, u, i, tê, á, erre, erre, á.
lines.en: G, U, I, T, A, R, R, A.

lines.speaker: Lúcia
lines.pt: Com dois erres. Muito bem, João!
lines.en: With two Rs. Very good, João!

lines.speaker: Camila
lines.en: Thank you, teacher! Bye!

grammar.title: The alphabet and the oral vowels
grammar.explanation:
Portuguese uses the same 26 letters as English, including k, w and y, which since the 2009 spelling reform are officially part of the alphabet. They appear mostly in foreign words and names. Each letter has a name, shown in the table. When you spell a name aloud you say these names, for example Pê, á, u, ele, ó for Paulo.

Portuguese spelling is far more regular than English. Once you know the rules in these notes, you can read almost any word aloud correctly. Every letter in a word is normally pronounced, except h, which is always silent, and u in qu and gu before e or i.

The five vowel letters give seven oral vowel sounds. The letter a is open, like the a in father. The letter e is either open, é, like the e in bed, or closed, ê, like the ay in say without the glide. The letter o is either open, ó, like the aw in law, or closed, ô, like the o in go without the w glide. The letters i and u are like the ee in see and the oo in moon. English vowels glide into a second sound, but Portuguese vowels are held steady and clean.

Unstressed vowels at the end of a word change in Brazilian Portuguese. A final unstressed a is a weak uh, as in casa. A final unstressed e sounds like ee, as in leite. A final unstressed o sounds like oo, as in livro. The letters p, t and k are said without the puff of air they have in English.

Diphthongs combine two vowel sounds in one syllable: ai like eye in pai, ei like ay in leite, oi like oy in boy, au like ow in now, eu like eh followed by oo, and ou, which is usually just a closed o.

rows: k before a, o, u; s before e, i
d; like j in jeep before i
g before a, o, u; zh before e, i
l; like w at the end of a syllable
m; nasalizes a vowel at the end of a syllable
n; nasalizes a vowel before a consonant
p without a puff of air
h-like or tap, depending on position
s or z, depending on position
t; like ch in cheese before i
sh, ks, z or s, depending on the word
like i, only in foreign words

examples.pt: Este é o pé do Paulo.
Este é o livro da Ana.

grammar.title: Nasal vowels and nasal diphthongs
grammar.explanation:
Portuguese has nasal vowels, which are vowels pronounced with air passing through the nose. English has a similar effect in words like song or sing, but Portuguese nasal vowels are clearer and the final consonant is not fully pronounced.

There are two ways to mark a nasal vowel in writing. The tilde, as in ã and õ, marks a nasal vowel directly: lã, irmã, põe. An m or n written after a vowel at the end of a syllable also nasalizes it: bom, sim, um, lindo, onde, tempo. In these cases the m or n is not a separate consonant, it only signals that the vowel is nasal. Do not close your lips on a final m.

Between two vowels, m and n are ordinary consonants. Compare ama (she loves, with a plain m) and lã (wool, nasal), or cano and canto. A nasal vowel is only formed when the m or n ends the syllable.

The nasal diphthongs deserve special attention because they are everywhere. The ending ão, as in pão, são and não, sounds like the ow in now said through the nose. The plural is usually ões: limão, limões. The ending ãe, as in mãe, sounds like the English word my said through the nose, and the plural is ães: mãe, mães. The ending õe, as in põe, sounds like oy in boy through the nose. When you practice, keep the sound in the nose and do not add an n or a g at the end.

In writing, the tilde also normally marks the stressed syllable, so you do not need a second accent: irmã is stressed on the last syllable.

rows: nasal ow, like now through the nose
nasal eye, like my through the nose
nasal oy, like boy through the nose
m or n before a consonant
m at the end of a word
nasalizes the vowel, lips stay open

grammar.title: Digraphs and sounds that depend on position
grammar.explanation:
A digraph is a pair of letters that stands for one sound. The digraph lh sounds like lli in million: filho. The digraph nh sounds like ny in canyon: banho. The digraph ch sounds like sh in shoe: chave. The digraph rr sounds like an English h in hat, and so does a single r at the start of a word or after n, l or s: carro, rua. A single r between vowels is a quick tap of the tongue, like the tt in American butter: caro. At the end of a syllable the r varies by region, from an h-like sound in Rio de Janeiro to a tapped or English-like r in parts of the interior, and speakers often drop it entirely at the end of infinitives such as falar.

The letters q and g change according to the vowel that follows. Qu before e or i is simply k with a silent u: queijo, quente. Gu before e or i is a hard g with a silent u: guitarra, guerra. Before a or o, the u in qu or gu is usually pronounced: água, quando. The letter c is like k before a, o, u and like s before e, i. The cedilla ç is always s and is used only before a, o, u: cabeça, açúcar. The letter g is a hard g before a, o, u and like the s in measure before e, i: gente. The letter j is always like the s in measure: hoje.

Some sounds depend on the position in the word. A single s between vowels is z: casa, mesa. At the start of a word or after a consonant it is s. A double ss is always s: passo. A final s is s in most of Brazil and sh in Rio de Janeiro and some other places: nós.

In most of Brazil the letters t and d before the vowel i, or before a final unstressed e, change: t sounds like ch in cheese and d like j in jeep. Tia is CHEE-uh, dia is JEE-uh, leite is LAY-chee and cidade is see-DAH-jee. Some regions, such as parts of the south and the northeast, use a plain t and d. A letter l at the end of a syllable sounds like w: Brasil, final, mil.

The letter x is the hardest. It sounds like sh at the start of words such as xícara and in words such as peixe, like ks in táxi, and like z in exemplo.

rows: rr, or r at the start of a word
g before e or i, and j
ch in cheese, j in jeep
l at the end of a syllable

examples.pt: Este é o filho do Carlos.

grammar.title: Stress and written accents
grammar.explanation:
Every Portuguese word with more than one syllable has one stressed syllable, and the rules for finding it are regular. Words that end in a, e, o, s, em or ens are stressed on the second to last syllable: casa, leite, livro, homem. Words that end in other consonants or in i or u are stressed on the last syllable: Brasil, falar, feliz, aqui. A written accent marks every exception to these rules, so when you see an accent, stress that syllable: café, você, ônibus, açúcar.

Accents also tell you about the quality of the vowel. The acute accent, agudo, marks stress and an open vowel for a, e and o: pé, avó, café. The circumflex, circunflexo, marks stress and a closed vowel for a, e and o: você, avô, ônibus. In practice a vowel with an accent is both stressed and either open or closed.

The tilde, til, marks a nasal vowel, as in mãe and pão, and normally also marks the stressed syllable, so words like irmã and irmão do not need another accent. The cedilla, cedilha, sits under c and gives an s sound: cabeça. The grave accent, as in à, is used for the crase, a fusion of the preposition a and the article a. You will meet it later, for example in times such as às nove horas.

Accents can change the meaning of a word. For example, pais means parents and país means country, and é means is while e means and. Always write the accents, because they are part of the spelling and not optional decoration.

rows: stress and open a, e, o
stress and closed a, e, o
crase, the fusion of a and a

culture.title: Accents, names and spelling out loud
culture.text:
Brazil is huge, and its accents are as varied as its geography. A carioca from Rio de Janeiro pronounces the final s like sh, so Brasil and mesmos have a hissing ending. In São Paulo the s stays a clean s, and in parts of the interior the r at the end of a syllable is a strong American-style r. In the south and in some northeastern cities, people say t and d without the ch and j sounds. None of these is wrong, and you will be understood anywhere if you follow the rules in this unit.

Brazilians love to give clues when they spell a name over the phone. Instead of just saying letter names, they often add a word for each letter: S de sapo, C de casa, B de bola, X de xícara. The first word can be any familiar noun, and the other person usually understands even if the word is unusual. If you need a name repeated, desculpa, como? is the standard polite request.

Many Brazilian names contain letters that are rare in older Portuguese spelling, such as the k in Kátia, the w in Wagner, and the y in Yasmin. They were once not officially part of the alphabet, but the 2009 spelling reform, put into effect in Brazil in 2009 and mandatory since 2016, made k, w and y official. Names also commonly carry nicknames, called apelidos, which are often short forms such as Zé for José or Gabi for Gabriela.

exercises.prompt: Which of these words has a nasal vowel?
exercises.explanation: The tilde in pão marks a nasal vowel. The ai in pai is an oral diphthong.

exercises.prompt: How is the digraph lh in 'filho' pronounced?
exercises.explanation: Lh is a single liquid sound, like lli in million.
In Portuguese ch sounds like sh in English.

exercises.prompt: In most of Brazil, the d in 'dia' sounds most like which English sound?
exercises.explanation: Before the vowel i, d becomes dj, so dia sounds like JEE-uh.

exercises.prompt: How is the final l in 'Brasil' pronounced?
exercises.explanation: An l at the end of a syllable sounds like w: bra-ZEEW.
The letter h is always silent in Portuguese.

exercises.prompt: What does the tilde in 'mãe' show?
exercises.explanation: The tilde marks a nasal vowel and usually also the stressed syllable.
Before e or i, qu sounds like k and the u is silent.
The letter L is called ele.
